clusters.name: Your stepfather Desmond settling into the home, 1987
clusters.reason: Around 1987 when you were fourteen, your stepfather moved in and you began secondary school: you grew distant from him while staying warm toward your dad, your dad's parents separated over a baby, and you made the city chess squad and hated it. These shifts in how you stood with your stepfather and the anxiety over chess sit close together as you adjusted to a new household and new school.

clusters.name: Your grandfather's return and death, 1989–1994
clusters.reason: Between 1989 when your grandfather came back into the family after years away and 1994 when you found your drive again in Portugal, events piled up: your family moved into the rebuilt house on Hollin Road where you liked late nights, you dropped chess and debate, your sister Tara was born, your grandfather died of a stroke when you were in your first term at the conservatory, you hurt your wrist and couldn't play, you fell into a deep drift at community college, and your cousin Bella was treated for melanoma. Your own shifts—the wrist injury, the fall in functioning, the loss of footing—sit alongside your grandfather's death and your mother's remarriage that autumn, and your functioning came back once you went to Portugal in early 1994.

clusters.name: Your split with Joelle, 1998–1999
clusters.reason: In 1998 you and Joelle became a couple; within a year your insomnia worsened though you were playing the best you ever had and winning competitions. You separated in July 1999 and started therapy with Victor that August. Your functioning rose alongside your insomnia rising, which marks a shift in the balance; the two moves together sit near the end of your relationship and its break.

clusters.name: Your grandmother's death and your depression, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Between September 2001 when you ran out of steam for performing and February 2004 when your grandmother died, the family moved through a long crisis around you. Your anxiety rose and functioning fell as you burned out; your grandmother was found to have bowel cancer around the same time; you had a disastrous audition and left Thornbury for Gull Harbour, then Fenwick with Marisol, and when that split in late 2003 you sank into a deep depression. You withdrew from your parents—you couldn't face them and they seemed a world away—while you relied on friends Corbin, Dale, Silas and Hamish; your dad and Corbin talked several times during your stay; you began swimming and asked your parents for help with therapy costs; you returned to Victor Halloran and your functioning began to climb. Your grandmother spent her final months in your parents' home and you dropped in briefly, hung over, on your way to the airport. Each shift of yours sits near shifts in the family around her illness and your move away, and the settling began once you started therapy in January 2004 and your functioning rose.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Lorna's death, 2008
clusters.reason: In January 2008 your grandmother Lorna died and around the same month your grandfather Clifford died; that summer you took four weeks building with Silas at Alder Creek before nursing school. You grew distant from your mother there—too drained for conversation—and she pressed you to visit, you kept the door shut on her, and once you moved to Marlow Sound in August for nursing school you stopped speaking to her altogether, a cutoff that held for roughly a year. Your aunt Imogen had a stroke with months of rehabilitation that winter. The distance between you and your mother piled up over those weeks and months; the cutoff settled once you moved to nursing school.

clusters.name: Your marriage to Wren and her family's life, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: From your marriage to Wren in March 2017 through the autumn of 2019, events clustered around you stepping into her family's closeness. In October 2019 she was swamped with events and you overfunctioned laying out a plan to settle her; her family talks all day with nothing happening to one that the others don't hear; at her mother's retirement party at the lake that October you woke from the small hours with no more sleep and could only pull back as the others rose, your worst sleep around her family because you feel you don't belong. Your sister Tara married James and had a baby on the way; your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis; your aunt Imogen's memory slipped and she lashed out when muddled; your uncle Gregory's health was checked; your job steadied and your anxiety dropped, but you feel constantly that you ought to drive your projects forward and started a sleeping pill. You aimed for shorter, more regular calls with your mother to soften the distance. Your anxiety rose and functioning fell as you moved into this marriage and its family, peaked around the lake weekend in late October, and began to settle as you planned more regular contact with your mother.

periods.name: the year you left home
periods.words: The first is the year I left home: I went off to the conservatory, hurt my wrist in the first term and couldn't play, dropped out and drifted at my mother's place, then spent a bleak spell at the community college shooting pool every night until an exchange in Portugal snapped me out of it and I tore through the rest of my coursework.

periods.name: the long slump
periods.words: The second is the long slump, roughly ages 27 to 29, when nothing at home felt right, I moved to Gull Harbour away from nearly everyone I knew, then followed Marisol to Fenwick, and when that fell apart I went under, a depression I only really climbed out of after nursing school.
